note: Sector-by-sector account of deployment across healthcare, automotive, finance and education, with the ethical and compute constraints stated alongside.
title: Industrial applications of large language models

reading.body:
This paper gives a sector-by-sector account of language model deployment across healthcare, automotive, finance, and education, stating the ethical and compute constraints specific to each.

Listing compute constraints alongside ethical ones, sector by sector, is a useful structure because the two are often conflated in general AI discussion. A finance deployment's constraints are mostly regulatory and ethical, while an automotive deployment's constraints are more about latency and the compute available on the vehicle itself. Treating these as separate axes, rather than one generic risk category, is what distinguishes this from a purely qualitative survey.

The paper does not rank sectors by adoption maturity or report deployment failure rates, only what constraints apply where.

explain_beginner: This paper is a broad survey asking a practical question, where are AI language models, the technology behind tools like ChatGPT, already being put to work across major industries today, not in theory but in actual reported use. The authors reviewed more than one hundred studies published between 2020 and 2024 and organized findings by sector. In hospitals, these systems help extract information from patient records and support diagnosis. Car manufacturers use them to predict when a vehicle needs maintenance before it breaks down and to power in car voice assistants. Banks use them to catch fraudulent transactions and automate customer service. Schools use them to personalize lessons and speed up grading. The paper's overall message is that these uses are real and already delivering value, but it pairs that with a clear warning, none of these deployments are free of cost or risk, since they depend on biased training data, real ethical tradeoffs, and heavy computing resources that not every organization can afford.
explain_business: For a business evaluating where LLMs already have proven, documented industrial use, as opposed to speculative use, this review's sector breakdown, healthcare, finance, automotive, and education, is a reasonable starting map, each backed by more than 100 reviewed studies from 2020 through 2024. The recurring caveat across every sector, that data bias, ethical exposure, and computing cost are still open problems rather than solved ones, means leadership should not treat sector level industry adoption alone as proof that a specific deployment is low risk. In practice this means budgeting for bias auditing and adequate compute infrastructure as standard costs of deployment in any of these four sectors now, not as optional extras, since the review found these same three constraints recurring regardless of which sector or specific use case was examined.
explain_practitioner: This is a systematic literature review that screened over 300 papers and analyzed more than 100 published between 2020 and 2024 across IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and Google Scholar, organizing findings into four industry sectors. In healthcare, cited applications include disease diagnosis support, patient data management, and automated radiology report generation. In finance, applications include fraud detection, risk assessment, and investor sentiment analysis. In automotive, applications include predictive maintenance and in vehicle virtual assistants, and in education, personalized learning and automated grading. Rather than presenting these as uniformly successful, the review consistently pairs each sector's applications with the same three recurring constraints found across the literature it surveyed, biased outcomes traceable to skewed training data, unresolved ethical questions around deployment, and the high computational resource requirements that determine which organizations can realistically operate these systems at production scale.
